content.text: Filling gaps with the column mean feels neutral, but it isn't. Every filled row gets the same value, the column's spread shrinks, and the fact that the value was missing disappears. When missingness carries information, the model loses it: in the example below, R² falls to 0.488. Keep a missing indicator, or use a model that handles NaN itself.
A retail team predicts yearly spend from a sign-up form where income is optional. They fill the blanks with
df.fillna(df.mean())
, train a linear regression and get an
R²

of 0.488. Predictions for their best customers come out consistently too low. Nobody suspects the one-line imputation, because the mean is the most neutral number there is. Except it isn't neutral: in this data, the customers who skip the income question are mostly the ones who earn the most.
The common misconception
Many developers treat mean imputation as a harmless way to make the data complete. That's understandable:

items.text: The mean is the best single guess when you know nothing else, and filling with it leaves the column's average unchanged.
unless told otherwise, and pandas makes it one line.
With a handful of gaps scattered at random, it really does little harm.
Dropping incomplete rows feels worse: it throws away whole customers, so filling looks like the conservative choice.

content.text: The half-truth: the mean preserves the column's average. It changes almost everything else, and it deletes a piece of information that was in the data all along:
which
values were missing.
What actually happens
Any filled value is a guess. The question is what the guess hides.
The same guess for every gap
Imputation
infers missing values from the known part of the data.
SimpleImputer

is univariate: it looks only at the column being filled, so every missing row gets exactly the same number. Those rows sit at the mean, adding nothing to the column's spread while counting toward its size, so the variance shrinks. They also carry no link to the target or to other columns, which dilutes the relationships the model is supposed to learn. Switching to the median doesn't change this: it's a different number, but still one number for every gap. Google's Machine Learning Crash Course puts it simply: imputed values are rarely as good as the actual values.
The mean of the answers isn't the mean of the gaps

The mean you fill with is computed from the people who answered. If whether someone answers depends on the answer itself, the two groups differ, and the fill value is wrong for exactly the rows it's used on. Statisticians call this "missing not at random". The script simulates it: high earners mostly skip the income question.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
income = rng.normal(50, 15, 2000)  # yearly income, thousands
age = rng.uniform(20, 65, 2000)
spend = 2 * income + 0.5 * age + rng.normal(0, 10, 2000)
skip = (income > 60) & (rng.random(2000) < 0.8)  # high earners skip it
X = pd.DataFrame({"income": np.where(skip, np.nan, income), "age": age})

fill, real = X["income"].mean(), income[skip].mean()
print(f"imputed {fill:.1f}, skipped rows really average {real:.1f}")
model = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="mean"), LinearRegression())
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
print(f"R^2 {cross_val_score(model, X, spend, cv=cv).mean():.3f}")
# imputed 44.6, skipped rows really average 68.7
# R^2 0.488

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
income = rng.normal(50, 15, 2000)  # yearly income, thousands
age = rng.uniform(20, 65, 2000)
spend = 2 * income + 0.5 * age + rng.normal(0, 10, 2000)
skip = (income > 60) & (rng.random(2000) < 0.8)  # high earners skip it
X = pd.DataFrame({"income": np.where(skip, np.nan, income), "age": age})

flagged = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True), LinearRegression())
boosting = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0)  # NaN-aware splits
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
for name, model in [("mean + indicator", flagged),
                    ("boosting, NaN kept", boosting)]:
    score = cross_val_score(model, X, spend, cv=cv).mean()
    print(f"{name:<18} R^2 {score:.3f}")
# mean + indicator   R^2 0.867
# boosting, NaN kept R^2 0.847

content.text: The imputer fills every gap with 44.6 thousand, while the people behind those gaps actually average 68.7. The model now sees high spenders with average incomes, can't explain them, and its R² drops to 0.488. Nothing in the pipeline raised an error or a warning. The data just quietly says something false.
The gap is a feature
The fix in the second script is one argument. With
add_indicator=True
SimpleImputer
appends a 0/1 column for every feature that had missing values during training, the output of scikit-learn's
MissingIndicator
. The linear model learns one more weight, for "income was skipped", which in this data means "probably earns a lot". R² climbs to 0.867.
The Crash Course recommends the same thing: a good dataset tells the model which values are imputed and which are actual, with a Boolean column such as
temperature_is_imputed
. scikit-learn's own imputation example adds the indicator to every strategy it compares.
Or let the model see the gap
HistGradientBoostingRegressor
and
HistGradientBoostingClassifier

accept NaN directly. At each split, the tree learns whether rows with a missing value should go left or right, based on which gives the better gain, and when missingness is predictive it can split on "missing or not" itself. With no imputer at all, it scores 0.847 here.

rows.text: Loses data, and skews the sample if gaps aren't random
Gaps are few and you have enough complete rows
One value for every gap; the median resists outliers
Gaps are rare and random; median for long tails
Keeps the "was missing" signal next to the fill
The default for linear and distance-based models
Estimate each gap from the other columns
Learns where missing rows go at each split

blocks.title: Ask the data whether the gaps matter

content.text: One line shows whether missingness is related to the target:
df.groupby(df["income"].isna())["spend"].mean()
. If the two groups differ clearly, the gap is information, and an indicator or a NaN-aware model will use it.

blocks.title: Fit the imputer on training rows only

content.text: df.fillna(df.mean())
before the train/test split computes the fill value from test rows too. scikit-learn's common pitfalls guide names
SimpleImputer
among the transformers where that kind of
data leakage
applies. At serving time the reverse bug appears: the fill value must be the training mean, not the mean of today's batch. A
Pipeline
stores it in the fitted imputer and applies it everywhere.

blocks.title: Indicators only cover what training saw

content.text: add_indicator
creates flags only for features that had missing values during
fit
. If a column is complete in training but has gaps in production, those rows are filled silently with no flag.
How to apply it in your project
Count missing values per column, and compare the target for rows with and without each value.

items.title: Ask why the value is missing

content.text: An optional field, a sensor that was down, or an event that never happened? "Never ordered" isn't an average order date; it deserves its own signal.
Use
add_indicator=True
for linear, distance-based and neural models, or a model with native NaN support such as
HistGradientBoosting
Median for skewed columns with outliers, a multivariate imputer when other columns can predict the missing one.
Cross-validate dropping, mean fill, fill plus indicator, and native NaN handling, with the imputer inside the pipeline so each fold fits it on training rows only.
Key takeaways

items.text: Mean imputation gives every gap the same value: the spread shrinks, and the fact that a value was missing is lost.
When missingness depends on the value, the mean of the answers is wrong for the gaps: 44.6 against 68.7 here.
A missing indicator turns the gap into a feature; in the example, R² rose from 0.488 to 0.867.
Fit imputers on training data inside a pipeline, and ship them with the model.
